prompts.flavor: Where the fire under the world breaks through. Some of them are only sleeping.
prompts.rules: Any named volcano, active, dormant or long extinct, on land, under the sea or on another world. Saying 'Mount' or 'Volcano' is optional. A mountain that was never a volcano doesn't count.

The tallest active volcano in Europe outside the Caucasus, and one of the busiest on Earth.
It last erupted in 1707, and pilgrims have climbed it for centuries.
Its 1883 eruption was heard nearly 5,000 km away, perhaps the loudest sound in recorded history.
Its 1980 eruption tore about 400 m off the top of the mountain.
Africa's highest mountain, and a dormant volcano.
A supervolcano beneath the world's first national park, founded in 1872.
Its ash closed much of Europe's airspace for days in April 2010.

The largest active volcano on Earth by volume.
Hawaiian tradition says the goddess Pele makes her home in its crater.
Its 1991 eruption cooled the whole planet by about half a degree for a year or so.
Its name means 'smoking mountain' in Nahuatl.
Its Bronze Age eruption may have helped bring down the Minoans, and is sometimes linked to Atlantis.
Spain's highest mountain, on Tenerife.

The southernmost active volcano on Earth, with a lake of lava in its crater.
A dormant volcano, where legend says Noah's Ark came to rest.
A dormant volcano, and the highest mountain in Europe by most counts.

Home to one of the largest lava lakes on Earth.

Spanish friars called it the mouth of hell, and planted a cross on its rim to keep the devil in.
The highest volcano on Earth, on the border of Chile and Argentina.

Its eruptions of 1730 to 1736 buried about a quarter of Lanzarote.
Portugal's highest mountain, on an island in the Azores.

Auckland's youngest volcano, risen from the sea about 600 years ago.

prompts.text: Name a city or town in Australia.
prompts.flavor: A thin ring of lights around a great dark middle. Name one of the lights.
prompts.rules: Any Australian city or town. Suburbs of the capitals do not count.

answers.lore: Said to be the only town in Australia whose name is a number. James Cook came ashore here in May 1770, his second landing on the continent.
A town of a few thousand south-east of Darwin, known for a giant boxing crocodile. Nobody is certain where the name came from, which suits it.

traps.reason: A suburb of a capital city. Name a city or town in its own right.

prompts.rules: Any named Australian river or major creek.

answers.lore: Alice Springs holds a boat race on it every year, in a dry bed, with the crews running. The regatta was cancelled in 1993 because the river had water in it.
Tasmania has a River Styx. It runs through a valley of swamp gums, the tallest flowering plants on Earth, some of them over 90 metres high.

traps.reason: Water, certainly, but not a river.

Which one? Name the river.

prompts.rules: Any sovereign country wholly or partly in Europe. The four nations of the United Kingdom count too.

aliases: Most Serene Republic of San Marino
answers.lore: The world's oldest surviving republic, by tradition founded in AD 301 by a stonemason hiding on a mountain. It is still run by two heads of state at once.

traps.reason: A territory or dependency, not a sovereign country.

answers.lore: Three atolls, about 1,500 people and no airport. In 2012 it became the first territory on Earth to run almost entirely on solar power.

prompts.rules: Any named river anywhere in the world.

answers.lore: The river that never finds the sea. It runs 1,600 kilometres inland from Angola and simply spreads out and vanishes into the Kalahari.

prompts.flavor: Still water keeps things. Ask anyone who has dropped something into one.
prompts.rules: Any named lake, loch or inland sea anywhere in the world.

answers.lore: A lake the size of Lake Ontario under nearly four kilometres of Antarctic ice, sealed off for millions of years. Russian drillers reached its surface in 2012.
Named in 1897 by explorer Frank Hann, who followed creeks inland hoping for fresh water and found a salt pan. It has been Kumpupintil Lake again since 2020.
A crater lake in Cameroon that, one night in 1986, released a cloud of carbon dioxide from its depths. It suffocated about 1,700 people as they slept.
